threads.topic: October 2025 was a midcycle top, not THE cycle top

tweets.text:
October 2025 wasn't the cycle top.

It was a midcycle top so weak it didn't even reach average power law.

The 2013 and 2019 midcycle tops both blew past it.

Here's what people are mourning that didn't actually happen 🧵
tweets.hook: October 2025 wasn't the cycle top.

tweets.text:
First, definitions.

A midcycle top is the local high partway through a cycle, not the cycle top itself.

In 2013, $BTC ran from ~$13 to ~$259 in Q1, peaked, sold off ~85%, then ran to ~$1,150 by year-end. That early peak was a midcycle top, not the cycle top.

The 2019 setup was the same shape.

$BTC ran from ~$3,200 in December 2018 to ~$13,800 in June 2019. Then it sold off into ~$3,800 by March 2020. Then it printed the actual cycle top at ~$69,000 in November 2021.

June 2019 was a midcycle top. The cycle top came later.

What both midcycle tops have in common: they blew well past average power law.

Average power law isn't a magic level. It's the regression of $BTC's lifetime price drawn through the middle.

Past midcycle tops cleared it convincingly. That's how you tell a real local high from noise.

October 2025 didn't reach it.

The "top" everyone is now mourning peaked below average power law. That's not a cycle top by any prior pattern. It's a local high inside a sideways structure.

If October had even matched the 2019 midcycle overshoot, $BTC would have printed well above $200k.

The four-year cycle zombies grieving October as the top are extrapolating from a midcycle high that didn't even break trend.

It would be like calling June 2019 the top of the 2017–2021 cycle.

Nobody serious did that then. Nobody serious should be doing it now.

The actual cycle top is still ahead.

When it prints, it'll be well above average power law, like every previous one. That's not a guess; it's the pattern every cycle has followed.

If you sold October expecting the bear, you sold a midcycle dip thinking it was a peak.
